title: Combination of Thin Lenses in Contact and Separated by a Distance
short_intro: The combination of thin lenses involves placing multiple lenses either in contact or separated by a finite distance along a common principal axis to modify the overall focal length and optical power. This technique is fundamental in optical instrument design to minimize aberrations and achieve desired magnification.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Derivation and application of equivalent focal length and power for two thin lenses in contact, sign convention, and magnification.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Equivalent focal length of two thin lenses separated by a distance d, cardinal points, system matrix representation, and combination of multiple lenses.

prerequisites: Refraction through spherical surfaces and Lens Maker's Formula
Real and virtual images formed by convex and concave lenses

concept_notes.heading: Equivalent Focal Length of Lenses in Contact
bullets: When two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> are kept in close contact, the combination acts as a single equivalent lens.
The reciprocal of the equivalent focal length (F) is equal to the algebraic sum of the reciprocals of individual focal lengths.
The total optical power P of the combination is the algebraic sum of individual powers: P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Magnification of Lenses in Contact
bullets: The total linear magnification produced by a system of thin lenses in contact is equal to the product of linear magnifications of individual lenses.
For an object placed at a distance u, the final image distance v satisfies 1/v - 1/u = 1/F.

concept_notes.heading: Two Thin Lenses Separated by a Distance
bullets: When two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> are separated by a distance d along their common principal axis, the equivalent focal length F is altered.
The separation d reduces the effective converging or diverging power compared to lenses in direct contact.
The position of the equivalent principal planes shifts depending on the separation distance d.

concept_notes.heading: Power and Matrix Approach for Lens Systems
bullets: Optical power is measured in dioptres (D) when focal length is expressed in meters.
In advanced PGT scope, translation and refraction matrices are used to compute the overall system matrix for separated lenses.
A combination of lenses can eliminate chromatic and spherical aberrations to a considerable extent (e.g., achromatic doublets).

derivations.title: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Thin Lenses in Contact
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> placed coaxially in contact.
steps: Let an object O be placed at a distance u from the combination on the principal axis.
The first lens alone would form an image at distance v<sub>1</sub> such that: \frac{1}{v_1} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f_1}.
This image acts as a virtual object for the second lens, forming the final image at distance v such that: \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{v_1} = \frac{1}{f_2}.
Adding the two equations eliminates v<sub>1</sub>: \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}.
Since the combination is replaced by a single equivalent lens of focal length F: \frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}.

derivations.title: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Lenses Separated by Distance d
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> separated by distance d < f<sub>1</sub>.
steps: Consider a ray parallel to the principal axis incident on the first lens of focal length f<sub>1</sub>.
It converges towards a point at distance f<sub>1</sub> behind the first lens in the absence of the second lens.
The second lens intercepts this ray at a distance d from the first lens, so the object distance for the second lens is u<sub>2</sub> = + (f<sub>1</sub> - d).
Applying the lens formula for the second lens: \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{f_1 - d} = \frac{1}{f_2}.
Solving for the equivalent focal length F from the optical center of the first lens gives the standard relation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ray Diagram for Two Convex Lenses in Contact
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two overlapping convex lenses on a principal axis showing a single incident ray refracting through both lenses to a common focus.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how the combined bending of light is greater than that of either individual lens, shortening the focal length.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding focal length changes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ray Diagram for Separated Lenses
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two convex lenses separated by distance d, showing parallel incident rays bending at the first lens, traveling across distance d, and undergoing further refraction at the second lens.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the shift in focal point and the formation of equivalent optical center.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT numericals regarding equivalent focal length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power vs Separation Distance Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear or non-linear decay curve of equivalent power P against separation distance d for two convex lenses.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that as separation d increases, the total power of two converging lenses decreases.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual interpretation of combined lens behavior.

solved_numericals.question: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +20 cm and -30 cm are placed in contact. Find the focal length and power of the combination.
solution_steps: Identify given values: f<sub>1</sub> = +20 cm = +0.2 m, f<sub>2</sub> = -30 cm = -0.3 m.

solved_numericals.question: Two thin convex lenses of focal lengths 30 cm and 20 cm are separated by a distance of 10 cm. Find the equivalent focal length of the combination.
solution_steps: Identify given values: f<sub>1</sub> = 30 cm, f<sub>2</sub> = 20 cm, d = 10 cm.
Apply the formula for separated lenses: 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub> - d / (f<sub>1</sub>f<sub>2</sub>).

solved_numericals.question: A convex lens of focal length 25 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. What is the nature and focal length of the combination?
solution_steps: Identify given values: f<sub>1</sub> = +25 cm (convex), f<sub>2</sub> = -20 cm (concave).
Interpret sign: Negative focal length indicates the combination behaves as a diverging (concave) lens.
solved_numericals.answer: Diverging lens with focal length -100 cm (-1 m)

assumptions_and_limitations.assumption: Lenses are assumed to be infinitely thin, so the thickness of each lens and the distance between their optical centers can be neglected in the contact formula.
assumptions_and_limitations.limitation: Fails for thick lenses where principal planes and optical centers do not coincide.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Adding two convex lenses increases the focal length of the system.
common_misconceptions.correct: Adding two convex lenses decreases the equivalent focal length.
common_misconceptions.why: Since 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub>, the reciprocal of the equivalent focal length increases, meaning F decreases and power increases.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The separation distance d is added to individual focal lengths.
common_misconceptions.correct: The separation distance is subtracted in the denominator term (-d / f<sub>1</sub>f<sub>2</sub>).
common_misconceptions.why: Separating converging lenses reduces the overall convergence of the ray bundle compared to direct contact.

quick_revision: For lenses in contact, 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub> and P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>.
Equivalent Power (In Contact): P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots + P_n
